summary.text: A comet is an icy small Solar System body that warms and releases gases when it passes close to the Sun, a process called outgassing.
That outgassing produces an extended atmosphere called a coma around the nucleus, and sometimes a tail of gas and dust.
Short-period comets are thought to originate in the Kuiper belt or its scattered disc, and long-period comets in the Oort cloud.

items.prompt: A comet far from the Sun is just a small icy body. What happens as it passes close to the Sun?

options.label: It cools and its ice hardens into a shell of rock
It warms and gives off gas that forms a cloud around its core
It starts to burn like a star and swells up
It collides with dust and picks up a thick cloud

items.explain: Warming near the Sun makes the comet release gases in outgassing, which forms a coma around the nucleus.

items.prompt: A comet takes millions of years to circle the Sun once. Where is it thought to have come from?

options.label: The Kuiper belt, in a disc beyond Neptune
The asteroid belt, between Mars and Jupiter
The scattered debris around Jupiter's moons
The Oort cloud, a spherical cloud of icy bodies

items.explain: Long-period comets are thought to originate in the Oort cloud, a spherical cloud of icy bodies.

items.prompt: Comet nuclei reflect less light than asphalt does. What best explains this?

options.label: Heat drives off light compounds, leaving dark organic ones
A coat of fresh black soot blown in from the Sun
A thin layer of black metal ore on the surface
Dense dark clouds of dust that block the light

items.explain: Solar heating drives off lighter volatiles and leaves behind larger organic compounds that are very dark, like tar.

items.prompt: How does a comet's very dark surface help it release gas?

options.label: It reflects most heat away so the ice stays frozen
It draws gas in from space and packs it onto the ice
It absorbs more of the heat that drives the outgassing
It shields the ice below from the stream of solar wind

items.explain: The low reflectivity of the surface makes it absorb the heat that drives outgassing.

items.prompt: Why did NASA's Deep Impact blast a crater on Comet Tempel 1?

options.label: To open a view into the comet's inside
To push it onto a safer path away from Earth
To make the coma brighter for telescopes
To collect dust and ice to bring back home

items.explain: Deep Impact blasted a crater on the comet to study its interior.

items.prompt: Asteroids are thought to form inside Jupiter's orbit and comets farther out, so why is the line between them blurred?

options.label: Comets and asteroids were found to share one origin
Main-belt comets and active centaurs have been discovered
Comets were found to orbit only inside Jupiter's orbit
Asteroids were all found to be made mostly of ice

items.explain: The discovery of main-belt comets and active centaur minor planets has blurred the distinction between asteroids and comets.

paragraphs.heading: A snowball that wakes up
paragraphs.text: A comet is a small, icy body, from our own Solar System or from between the stars, that warms up and starts giving off gas when it passes close to the Sun. That release of gas is called outgassing. It wraps the solid core, called the nucleus, in a wide atmosphere that gravity does not hold in place, known as the coma. Sometimes a tail of gas and dust is also blown out from the coma. Sunlight and the solar wind, streaming out from the Sun, act on the nucleus to cause all of this.

paragraphs.heading: Small core, huge coma
paragraphs.text: A nucleus is loosely packed ice, dust and small rocky bits, from a few hundred metres to tens of kilometres across. Long-period comets tend to be the bigger ones, usually 4 to 20 km wide, while most short-period comets measure 1.5 to 5 km. The coma around that small core can grow to 15 times the width of Earth, and the tail can reach past one astronomical unit. A comet that is close and bright enough can be seen without a telescope, stretching up to 30° across the sky, the width of 60 Moons.

paragraphs.heading: Dirty snowball or icy dirtball
paragraphs.text: A nucleus mixes rock, dust and water ice with frozen carbon dioxide, carbon monoxide, methane and ammonia. Fred Whipple's model made them famous as dirty snowballs. But after NASA's Deep Impact probe struck Comet 9P/Tempel 1 in July 2005, icy dirtballs may be the better name. Work from 2014 compared comets to deep fried ice cream: a dense, crystal-like icy surface mixed with organic compounds, over colder and less dense ice inside. The surface itself is usually dry, dusty or rocky, which hints that the ices lie under a crust several metres thick.

paragraphs.heading: Darker than asphalt
paragraphs.text: The outer surface of a nucleus has a very low albedo, meaning it reflects very little light, so comets are among the darkest objects in the Solar System. The Giotto probe found that Halley's Comet reflects about four percent of the light hitting it, and Deep Space 1 found that Comet Borrelly reflects less than 3.0%; asphalt, by comparison, reflects seven percent. The Sun's heat drives off the lighter frozen compounds and leaves behind larger organic ones that are very dark, like tar. Because the surface is so dark, it soaks up the heat that powers outgassing.

paragraphs.heading: Where comets come from
paragraphs.text: Most comets travel on long, stretched-out oval orbits, taking anywhere from several years to possibly millions of years to go around once. Short-period comets come from the Kuiper belt and the scattered disc beyond Neptune. Long-period comets are thought to come from the Oort cloud, a ball-shaped swarm of icy bodies reaching from past the Kuiper belt to halfway to the nearest star. Passing stars and the galactic tide nudge them toward the Sun. Hyperbolic comets may swing through the inner Solar System only once before being thrown out into interstellar space.

paragraphs.heading: Counting and visiting comets
paragraphs.text: As of November 2021, astronomers knew of 4,584 comets. That is only a tiny share of the total, since the Oort cloud may hold about a trillion comet-like bodies. Roughly one comet a year can be seen with the naked eye, though many are faint, and especially bright ones are called great comets. Robot probes have gone to see them up close: NASA's Deep Impact blasted a crater in Comet Tempel 1 to study its insides, and the European Space Agency's Rosetta became the first mission to set a robot lander down on a comet. In 2009, scientists confirmed the amino acid glycine in comet dust brought back by NASA's Stardust mission.

paragraphs.heading: The long-haired star
paragraphs.text: The word comet comes through Old English and Latin from the Greek komētēs, meaning wearing long hair. In Greek it already meant a long-haired star, a comet, and its root word for the hair of the head was also used for a comet's tail.
